structure.title: 5. Results for child mortality (baseline, heterogeneity, robustness)

observations.statement: The design is named as a judge-assignment IV: quasi-random judge assignment combined with across-judge variation in removal tendency. The estimand is described as the LATE for compliers, children who could have received another decision under a different judge, with MTE-based parameters added.

Exclusion is argued institutionally: the judge makes a single binary decision, has minimal contact with the family, and all other care decisions rest with the local child welfare committee. The paper contrasts this with caseworker instruments whose exclusion is harder to defend.

The assignment process is described in detail from court staff interviews at several courts (rotating assignment within departments), with the junior-judge exception stated and later addressed by exclusion checks.

The four IV assumptions are laid out in separate subsections (relevance, random assignment, exclusion, monotonicity), each with its own empirical evidence. Strong versus average monotonicity are distinguished with citations to recent methodological work.
Raw event-time plots around the judgment are shown to explain why an event-study design is unsuitable here (selection into removal and pre-judgment spikes), motivating the IV design.

Primary data are court judgments hand-collected from courts and archives, transcribed with automated and manual methods with manual verification, then linked by the statistics agency via personal identity numbers to death, patient, crime, education and population registers.

Coverage of court documents is described by period: universal coverage in the later period, a subset of courts in an intermediate period, and a single court department in the earliest years. Register windows are given per register.

The unit is child-by-case. Exclusions are listed in order with reasons: children not observed in registers, missing instrument, and court-by-year cells with a single active judge. Judges with few cases are dropped to limit measurement error in the instrument.

Three named analysis samples are defined by outcome horizon and age (an all-ages sample, a year-19 sample, and an age-restricted sample); the age cutoff is justified by the youngest observed suicide or overdose age.
Attrition from emigration is noted for main tables, and selective attrition is tested by regressing a missing indicator on the instrument, with results in an appendix table and a footnote pointer.
A placement register with known underreporting is described and explicitly excluded from the main analysis, used only for mechanisms.

The instrument is the leave-out mean removal rate of the judge, leaving out the entire case (all siblings) to avoid a mechanical link; a formula is given. It is computed on all available cases, not just the analysis sample.
An alternative yearly leave-out instrument is checked against the main instrument in a footnote, and alternative instrument definitions appear in appendix first-stage tables.

Treatment is an indicator for a court-ordered removal. Outcomes are cumulative event indicators by a fixed age or by month t after judgment; crime is dated by offence date rather than conviction date, using the first day for multi-day offences.
Mechanism splits use random-forest predicted risks (of moving, placement instability, placement type) and a survey-based welfare committee quality score, with definitions delegated to Appendix A.

The main table stacks estimator rows (OLS without controls, OLS with controls, complier-reweighted OLS, reduced form, IV with FE only, IV with controls) across outcome columns, and reports dependent mean, control complier mean, N, the sample name, and AR p-values and confidence sets per column.

Table notes state that court-by-year fixed effects are in all but the no-control OLS row and that controls are the child and parent characteristics listed in the descriptive table; secondary tables show control inclusion as Yes/No rows.
A complier-reweighted OLS row is reported, with the weighting procedure (extreme judges, random-forest risk quartiles, relative complier shares) described in a footnote.
Standard errors are clustered at the case level because judges are assigned to cases that may contain siblings; the choice is supported with citations to clustering guidance.
observations.quote: I cluster the standard errors at the case level

observations.statement: Anderson-Rubin tests and identification-robust confidence sets are reported alongside conventional standard errors, citing weak-instrument guidance; figures use AR confidence bands.
A Monte Carlo power calculation is described in a footnote: mortality risk is predicted by random forest, shifted by the estimated effect, and the IV regression re-run on simulated draws.

The first stage is shown graphically in the main text (residualized instrument histogram with local polynomial fit) and in appendix tables with and without controls, reporting effective F-statistics; the first-stage magnitude is benchmarked against the judge-IV literature.

A two-column randomization table regresses removal and then the instrument on the same background variables, reporting joint F-statistics, so that predictors of treatment can be contrasted with their (null) relation to the instrument. Additional randomization tests are in an appendix table.

A joint test of exclusion, random assignment and strong monotonicity following Frandsen et al. is reported per main outcome in an appendix table, and the instrument is shown uncorrelated with case and placement characteristics.
Monotonicity is probed by estimating first stages in observable subsamples and with an instrument computed outside the subsample, checking that all are positive.

Reduced-form plots overlay actual outcomes and predicted outcomes (from covariates) against the instrument, using binned means and local polynomial fits, to assess linearity and conditional randomization.
Complier characteristics are compared with the analysis sample in an appendix table and used to discuss why OLS and IV differ and whom the LATE covers.

A nonlinear two-stage residual inclusion estimator with probit stages is reported in the appendix as an alternative to linear 2SLS for binary and imbalanced treatment and outcome, with a literature discussion of why 2SLS remains the baseline.

Robustness to sample, specification and instrument construction choices, and to dropping each court, is summarised in one short paragraph with appendix tables; junior-judge exclusions are also mentioned in the background section.
observations.locator: Section 5.3; Tables D4 and D5; Section 2.1

observations.statement: Subgroup effects by child characteristics are reported in an appendix table with Wald tests of equality across groups.
MTE curves over unobserved resistance and propensity score common support (after trimming tails) are plotted; ATE, ATT and ATUT approximations are given with a caution about limited support.

Mechanism heterogeneity uses interactions of removal with above/below-median predicted-risk indicators, instrumented by the corresponding interactions with the judge instrument, and reports differences between groups.
IV effects are interpreted relative to the control complier mean rather than the overall dependent mean, and both are printed in the table.
An implied additional deaths calculation is worked through using the complier share, assumptions about never-takers, and the lower bound of the AR set as a conservative alternative.

The paper cautions that the instrument shifts removal probability over a limited range, so the binary-treatment interpretation requires linear extrapolation; it reports the effect without extrapolation and probes linearity via first-stage and reduced-form graphs.
Peer-effect results are expressed as the effect of a one standard deviation change in exposure relative to the mean risk for the relevant group.

Mechanisms open with a qualitative investigation: the author contacted welfare committees for case notes and death investigations of removed children who died, interviewed caseworkers where possible, and coded contributing factors.

Four pre-announced channels (disruption, care conditions, peers, parents) are each tested with intermediate outcomes (healthcare use, crime, schooling), predicted-risk heterogeneity, and parent outcomes; the disruption channel is explicitly not ruled out despite null splits.

Peer effects are estimated with a different design from a companion paper (facility-by-year fixed effects, within-facility temporal variation), re-run on the court-removed subpopulation, with an identifying-assumption test in the appendix.

Timing patterns (deaths around the 18th birthday, summer months) are used descriptively to distinguish anticipation from transition-to-adulthood channels, with a stated inability to separate summer break from summer in general.

Reporting biases in healthcare and crime records are discussed (caregiver propensity to seek care, supervision effects on detection, prosecutor practices), with an argument for why hospitalizations are less affected.

The conclusion states limitations: only court-ordered placements are studied, sample restrictions raise mean age, and compliers differ on some characteristics, which together threaten external validity.

A dedicated comparison section relates the results to North American studies through differences in institutions, service eligibility, placement rates and composition, rather than through statistical reconciliation.

The descriptive table shows child, parent and judge characteristics for each analysis sample side by side with a registry-wide comparison column, and separately for children who die, with counts of unique judges, cases, children and parents.
Tables use three-level significance stars, and notes state the sample name, fixed effects, control set, and case-level clustering.

Dynamic effects are shown as IV point estimates on cumulative outcomes by month since judgment with AR confidence bands, conditioning on being alive and in the country; the same layout is reused for mortality, healthcare and crime.
Raw monthly event probabilities are plotted by treatment status around the judgment, and reduced-form binned means are overlaid on kernel fits with the kernel, degree and bandwidth stated in notes.

Appendix tables are lettered by appendix (A definitions, B background and diagnostics, C attrition, D results), and a single main-text results table is complemented by many appendix tables referenced inline.

The introduction previews the main results and mechanism findings, then gives several contribution paragraphs positioning the work against child-protection, mental-health and judge-IV literatures, without a roadmap paragraph.

Order is background, data (including instrument construction), methodology with one subsection per assumption, mortality results with heterogeneity and a short robustness subsection, then a long mechanisms section, a comparison section and conclusion.

The institutional section is long and organised around the same four channels later tested as mechanisms (care conditions, healthcare, quality), so that background reads as motivation for the mechanism tests.
A data availability statement points to a Zenodo replication package DOI, and the package is also cited as a reference for data collection details.
Register data were linked and delivered by Statistics Sweden and health, crime and institutional agencies, acknowledged by name; no access procedure is given in the text.
Ethical approval by the national ethical review authority is stated in the acknowledgments.
observations.quote: approved by the Swedish Ethical Review Authority

observations.statement: Appendices A to D are cited throughout but are supplementary material not included in the article text; only the main text was available to read.

gaps: No discussion of few-cluster or multiple-testing concerns despite many outcomes.
No software named in the text (code is Stata per the replication package).
No data access procedure for the Swedish register data is described.
Appendices A to D (variable definitions, diagnostics, attrition, appendix results) are supplementary and not in the text file.
No roadmap paragraph in the introduction.

reading.note: All 37 pages read, including references (pages 33 to 37). Appendices A to D are online supplementary material and are not part of the text; they were not available.
